note: Tagalog writes the k sound with k, never c: kape, kah-PEH (coffee).
g stays hard before i and e, as in go: gising, ghee-SEENG (awake).
sy before a vowel is said sh: pasensya, pah-SEHN-shah (patience; sorry). siya (he, she) is usually said shah too.
dy is said j: medya, MEH-jah (half), as in alas-singko y medya (half past five).
ñ is said ny, as in canyon. It turns up in names and Spanish words: Santo Niño, SAHN-toh NEE-nyoh.
si-siw: iw is an ee that ends in w. Stress the first syllable.
ka-hoy: oy as in boy. Stress the first syllable.
sa-baw: aw sounds like the ow in cow. Stress the last syllable.
ka-la-baw: three syllables, each with one vowel sound. Stress the last.
pa-a: two vowels side by side are two syllables.
ta-i-nga: here a and i are two syllables, not the ay of eye; nga starts with the ng of singer. Casual: tenga.
ngi-pin: ng starts the word. Stress the last syllable.
ung-goy: ngg is the ng of singer, then a hard g; oy as in boy.
gi-ta-ra: g stays hard before i; r is one quick tap.
bun-dok: a consonant can close a syllable. Stress the last syllable.
bu-lak-lak: three syllables. Stress the last.
tso-ko-la-te: ts is ch, and k is written where English has c.
dy is said j. One syllable, so the line has no capitals.
ra-dyo: r is one quick tap, dy is said j. Stress the first syllable.
ma-li: stress the last syllable; the word ends in a catch.
pu-sa: two open syllables. Stress the first.
u-lan: stress the last syllable.
pu-no: stress the first syllable. Stressed at the end, with a catch, it means full.
